title: Derivation Depth Exposes Reasoning Failures in Tool-Augmented Music Analysis

paper.title: Derivation Depth Exposes Reasoning Failures in Tool-Augmented Music Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Audio-language models remain unreliable at extracting basic musical properties from audio, motivating pipelines that place a music information retrieval (MIR) tool between the audio and the model. The tool reports measurements such as keys, chords, and structural similarity, and the model is expected to derive the answer. We test whether it can. Holding the musical information fixed, we vary derivation depth: the number of reasoning steps between the tool output and the answer. When the report states the conclusion, all five models score near 100 % 100\% , and they follow it even when it is wrong. One step away, accuracy drops. On modulation, open models fall to 57 57 – 81 % 81\% , although they answer that single step correctly when asked directly, and reach 0 % 0\% at greater depths. Frontier models degrade less, but still degrade. Adding the audio does not recover the loss. The bottleneck in tool-augmented music analysis is not access to musical information but reasoning from it, so tool design must account for how much derivation it leaves to the model. Project Page

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Audio-language models offer a natural interface for music analysis, but achieve only near-chance performance when recovering basic musical properties directly from audio [ 1 , 12 ] . A promising alternative is to augment them with music information retrieval (MIR) tools. Rather than requiring the language model to recognize every property from audio directly, an MIR system can provide keys, chords, structural similarity, or other measurements, which the model then uses to answer higher-level musical questions. Classical MIR methods already provide many such measurements [ 3 , 7 , 8 ] , and recent tool augmented audio systems report substantial gains from incorporating external evidence [ 16 , 10 ] . However, MIR tools often return intermediate measurements rather than the answer itself. For example, a tool may return “new key: D major”, while the user’s question asks whether the modulation is to a major or minor key: even this requires the language model to recognize that D major is a major key. Existing tool-augmented evaluations measure only final accuracy, which conflates tool errors with failures to reason over tool output. We isolate the second: given the right musical information, can the model derive the answer. To isolate this capability, we introduce derivation depth : the number of inferential steps needed to get from a tool’s measurement to the answer, ranging from zero, where the report already states the conclusion, to several, where it gives only a raw measurement. Figure 1: Setup and failure modes. (a) The model answers a musical question from the audio and an MIR tool’s output. (b) It follows a stated conclusion even when wrong (top), and fails to derive the conclusion from intermediate output such as the home key and secondary dominant (bottom). Fig. 1 shows the setup and the two failures we measure. We evaluate five audio-language models across five music-analysis tasks, using controlled stimuli and real recordings. We additionally test whether the original audio can compensate for failed derivation, probe the musical knowledge required at each depth, and deliberately invert tool conclusions to measure whether models verify or simply follow them. The results expose a reliability gap. When the tool states the conclusion directly, models are nearly perfect; when that conclusion is deliberately inverted, they follow the incorrect statement just as readily. More importantly, even one elementary reasoning step is enough to substantially reduce accuracy. On modulation, replacing “the new key is major” with “new key: D major” drops the three open models from 100 % 100\% to 57 57 – 81 % 81\% , despite all three identifying the same major/minor fact with 100 % 100\% accuracy when asked directly. Providing the chord instead drops accuracy to 0 0 – 26 % 26\% , and providing only its pitches reduces it to 0 % 0\% . Thus, the difficulty arises before long reasoning chains are needed: models can possess the required musical knowledge yet fail to apply it to the tool output. The effect persists with acccess to audio and on real GuitarSet recordings. For modulation, the answer never becomes decodable inside the network. For structure, it emerges mid-network but fades before the output. This limits a natural workaround: writing out an intermediate step helps when the network forms the information, but does not rescue deeper derivations and can discard what the final answer needs. Together, these results identify a missing capability in tool-augmented music analysis: reliable reasoning over tool outputs . Improving the MIR tool alone is insufficient when the downstream model cannot reliably transform its measurements into the requested conclusion. In summary, our contributions are a controlled framework for measuring derivation depth , evidence that even elementary derivations fail despite available musical knowledge , and mechanistic evidence distinguishing conclusions that are never formed from those that are formed but lost before output .

sections.heading: 2 Method and Experiments
sections.text: Experiments fix the musical fact and varies only how it reaches the model: report format, audio, and reasoning distance.

sections.heading: 2.1 Setup
sections.text: Tasks. Each task is a minimal pair: two versions of a piece differing in exactly one musical property, which isolates that property as the sole determinant of the correct answer. The five tasks are cadence (authentic vs. deceptive), modulation (new major vs. minor key), scale (Lydian vs. Ionian, one note apart), motif (transposed return vs. a new motif) and structure (ABA vs. through-composed). Each targets a property a standard MIR tool reports. All battery items are synthetic: short scores written to exhibit exactly one property are generated programmatically as MIDI and rendered to audio with FluidSynth (TimGM6mb General MIDI soundfont, piano), and the template report is filled from the known score, so ground truth is exact. Each task has N = 6 N{=}6 compositions rendered at up to five transpositions between − 6 -6 and + 6 +6 semitones, giving up to 30 30 pairs per task ( 23 23 for scale). Table 1: One modulation item rendered in each tool-output format. Colors group formats: verdict ( green ), value or prose ( blue ), raw tool output ( rose ). Style Example tool output F1 Verdict “The piece modulates at bar 9 to a new MAJOR key (G major).” 𝐅𝟏 ¯ \overline{\mathbf{F1}} Verdict (flip) “The piece modulates at bar 9 to a new MINOR key (A minor).” F2 Key–value bars9_16_key: G major F3 Prose “From bar 9 the harmony re-centers on G major, a major key (pivot chord D7).” F4 Tool output chord_report: bar1=C, bar2=F, …, bar9=D7, …, bar16=G F5 Output + noise F4 + + tempo_bpm=104, first_key=C major, rms_db=-15.5 F6 JSON {"chords_by_bar": {"1": "C", …, "9": "D7", …}} Measurement formats. For each item we express the same musical information in six forms that reflect how an MIR measurement may appear in a tool-augmented system (Table 1 ). F1 and F3 state the conclusion; F2 gives the single value it follows from; F4 to F6 give the full tool output with increasing clutter (F5) and structure (F6). F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} states the wrong conclusion in F1’s form, to test whether a model follows the report even against the correct answer. Derivation ladder. To order the formats by reasoning distance, we generate 72 72 items per task in which the same fact is reported at four depths: d0 states the conclusion; d1 gives the fact one step away (for modulation, the home and new key); d2 gives the evidence for that fact (the pivot chord); d3 gives only its constituents (the chord’s pitches). Items vary key and harmonic relation rather than transposition, so every report is distinct, and intervals for the ladder resample items. Real tool output and real recordings. We rebuild all six formats for modulation and structure from a running librosa [ 8 ] analyzer on the same audio, so the report is a real tool’s output rather than a template. Separately, on 60 60 GuitarSet [ 14 ] recordings with expert key annotations, we ask for the key from audio alone, with the annotation supplied as the tool output, and with a deliberately wrong annotation. Models and input conditions. We test three open-weight models run locally, Qwen2.5-Omni [ 15 ] , Music Flamingo (MF) [ 4 ] , and Audio Flamingo 3 (AF3) [ 5 ] , and two API models, Gemini 2.5 Flash [ 2 ] and Gemini 3.6 Flash [ 6 ] . We run every format in two conditions: no-audio, where the model sees only the measurement, which isolates whether it can read the measurement on its own; and audio-crossed, where the model also gets the audio, which tests whether audio helps when reasoning from the measurement fails. Scoring. Each test item is a matched pair containing both alternatives of the task (e.g., one major-key modulation and one minor-key modulation). A pair is counted as correct only when the model answers both members correctly. Because the two members have opposite correct answers, a model that always gives the same response is correct on at most one of them and scores 0 % 0\% pair accuracy; chance is 25 % 25\% . We report 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples over base compositions. We resample compositions rather than individual transpositions because transpositions of the same composition are not independent. We validated automatic keyword scoring against 100 manually scored responses, achieving κ = 0.90 \kappa=0.90 agreement. Knowledge probes. To separate a missing fact from a failure to combine facts already present, we ask each fact the modulation ladder needs alone, with terse answer-only questions ( 48 48 items each): whether a named key is major or minor (needed at d1); which key a dominant seventh resolves to and whether a scale degree is major or minor (d2); which chord a set of pitches spells (d3). To check that a terse probe does not understate knowledge, the d2 rule is also asked with the rule stated, as multiple choice, and with reasoning permitted. Mechanistic probes. Behavioral failure alone cannot tell us whether Qwen2.5-Omni never computes an answer or computes one it fails to use. We test this on two conditions already in the behavioral evaluation: conclusion stated (modulation d0, structure F1) and derivation required (modulation d2, 72 72 items; structure F4, 30 30 items). Since the derivation-required condition often declines to answer, we append a fixed continuation (“The new key is”, “The third section”) and read the residual stream at the answer position. A logit lens [ 9 ] projects that stream through the output head at every layer, tracking the model’s preference between the two candidate answers: a conclusion that is present should be decodable before the final layer. Activation steering [ 13 ] tests whether the state that encodes the correct conclusion can rescue a failing derivation: for modulation, we inject the mean hidden-state difference between the two conditions, computed leave-one-out over items, into the derivation-required forward pass at one of seven layers and several strengths, and measure accuracy. As a control, we also state the required musical rule in the prompt (Fig. 3 ). Two-call mitigation. If a derivation is never performed, forcing it into the transcript should help. We test this with a two-call procedure: in the first call, the model states what the measurement says and what it indicates; in the second call, it answers using only its own first-call statement, with the original measurement withheld. This differs from ordinary chain-of-thought prompting [ 1 ] , where the model can still fall back on the original evidence.

sections.heading: 3 Results and Discussion
sections.text: Finding 1. Models follow stated conclusions, even when they are wrong. When the tool output states the conclusion (F1/F3), all models are near-perfect. But when we deliberately flip that conclusion in F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} , accuracy falls to 0 % 0\% for every model, the frontier models included (Table 2 , last column): each follows the incorrect statement, even when audio is available. Thus, the models read the tool output but do not reliably verify its conclusion. Table 2: Format profile, pair accuracy (%), structure and modulation pooled ( n = 60 n{=}60 pairs, 12 12 compositions). Verdict = = F1/F3, Measurement = = F2/F4/F5/F6. Δ \Delta is verdict minus measurement, no audio [95% CI] and with audio. F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} is the flipped verdict (pair accuracy; 0 0 means every pair followed the wrong statement). Model Verdict Meas. Δ \Delta no audio Δ \Delta + + aud. F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} Qwen2.5-Omni 100 36 64 [56,72] 48 0 Music Flamingo 100 35 65 [48,83] 67 0 Audio Flamingo 3 100 35 65 [48,83] 58 0 Gemini 2.5 Flash 100 85 15 [9,21] 21 0 Gemini 3.6 Flash 100 90 10 [4,17] 15 0 Finding 2. Accuracy falls with the distance between tool output and answer; one reasoning step is enough. The format profile. The gap appears as soon as the tool provides measurements rather than the answer itself (Table 2 ). In the no-audio condition, open-model accuracy drops from 100 % → ∼ 35 % 100\%\to{\sim}35\% , while the Gemini models show a smaller but consistent drop. Providing the relevant tool output is therefore not sufficient; performance depends on how much reasoning remains between that output and the answer. Modulation F2 reveals one confound: it gives the new key but not the home key, so the output alone does not establish that a modulation occurred. We therefore use a controlled derivation ladder in which every rung contains sufficient information, while only the number of reasoning steps changes. The derivation ladder. We fix the musical fact and vary how many reasoning steps separate the tool output from the answer (Fig. 2 , Table 3 ). On modulation, all three open models score 100 % 100\% when the report states the conclusion (d0). Replacing the conclusion with the new key, “D major,” leaves one step: recognizing that D major is a major key. Accuracy falls to as low as 57 % 57\% . Giving the secondary dominant instead (d2) drops it to 0 0 – 26 % 26\% , at or below chance. Giving only its pitches (d3) drops it to 0 % 0\% . At every depth the question is the same, whether the new key is major or minor, and so is the answer: major (D major). Cadence and structure follow the same trend, though the step where models fail differs by task. The limitation appears before any long chain of reasoning. One elementary step between tool output and answer already costs up to 43 43 points. The frontier models split on the hardest chain: Gemini 2.5 Flash collapses at d2 like the open models ( 15 % 15\% ), while Gemini 3.6 Flash, which reasons internally before answering, holds 86 86 and 82 % 82\% at d2 and d3; both are at or near 100 % 100\% on every cadence and structure rung. Figure 2: Pair accuracy against derivation depth on three tasks, no audio, n = 72 n{=}72 independent items each. Depth zero states the conclusion; each further step withholds one inference. Open models in color, frontier models in gray; dotted line is chance ( 25 % 25\% ). Finding 3. The first-step failure is not a knowledge gap A natural explanation for the depth drop is missing music-theory knowledge. We test the required intermediate facts directly (Table 3 , right block). At d1, all three open models identify whether a named key is major or minor with 100% accuracy, yet score as low as 57% when that same fact must be used to answer the modulation question. Thus, even the first-step failure reflects difficulty applying available knowledge to the tool output, not simply missing knowledge. At deeper levels, both effects appear: some models lack the required theory, while others know the intermediate facts but still fail to combine them. The derivation failure therefore cannot be explained by knowledge gaps alone. Table 3: Modulation: derivation ladder beside the knowledge each depth needs. Color marks the reasoning required: none , one step , two or more . Audio, no report : pair accuracy from the clip alone (chance 25 25 ). Ladder : pair accuracy (%) without / with audio ( n = 72 n{=}72 items; one number when both agree). Knowledge : the fact each depth needs, asked alone ( n = 48 n{=}48 per question for the open models, 37 37 for the scale-degree question; n = 144 n{=}144 for Gemini): d1, is a named key major or minor; d2, which key a dominant seventh resolves to / whether a scale degree is major or minor; d3, which chord a set of pitches spells. G2.5F/G3.6F: Gemini 2.5/3.6 Flash. Audio, Ladder, without/with audio Knowledge, asked alone Model no report d0 d1 d2 d3 d1 d2 d3 Qwen 17 100 76/89 26/25 0/0 100 19/59 0 AF3 0 100 81/8 0/0 0/0 100 17/100 12 MF 0 100 57/81 6/3 0/1 100 85/59 19 G2.5F 17 100 100 15/43 21/32 100 83/100 18 G3.6F 13 100 100 86/81 82/47 100 85/100 23 Finding 4. Audio does not rescue derivation, and the gap persists on real recordings. Providing the original audio does not recover failures at deeper derivation depths (Table 3 , left). We then test whether the same pattern holds when the tool output comes from a running librosa analyzer [ 8 ] rather than the template report, and whether it carries over to real GuitarSet recordings [ 14 ] (Table 4 ). When the analyzer is correct, conclusion-style outputs remain near-perfect, while measurement-style outputs reduce accuracy by 54–73 points across the three open models. When the analyzer gives an incorrect conclusion, the models follow it rather than correcting it from the audio, and on GuitarSet every model follows a wrong key annotation (33–100% of the time) even though the open models identify the key from audio alone in 50–62% of recordings and the Geminis in only 8–15%. Thus, neither access to the audio nor real tool output nor real recordings removes the derivation gap. Table 4: Beyond the template report. Audio, no report : accuracy from the recording alone (synthetic: pair accuracy, chance 25 25 ; GuitarSet: open-ended key identification on 60 60 recordings, chance about 4 4 ). Δ \Delta : verdict minus measurement formats, without / with audio, for the template report and for a running librosa analyzer on the same synthetic audio (analyzer correct on 56 56 of 60 60 pairs in the open-model runs, 54 54 in the Gemini runs). Wrong verdict followed : how often a wrong tool conclusion was adopted (synthetic F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} ; the analyzer’s wrong pairs; a wrong key annotation on GuitarSet). Audio, no report Δ \Delta verdict − - meas. Wrong verdict followed (%) Model Synth. Guitar Templ. Librosa F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} Librosa Guitar Qwen 21 55 64/48 60/57 100 100 63 MF 0 62 65/67 73/52 100 100 100 AF3 0 50 65/58 54/61 100 100 33 G2.5F 17 8 15/21 33/23 100 100 100 G3.6F 13 15 10/15 12/22 100 100 100 Finding 5. Derivation fails either because the conclusion is never formed or because it is lost. The mechanistic probes reveal two distinct failure modes (Fig. 3 ). For modulation, the correct answer never becomes reliably decodable at any layer when derivation is required. Activation steering does not recover it (Qwen moves from 25 % 25\% to at most 29 % 29\% across seven layers), and stating the required rule in the prompt moves the open models nowhere (Qwen 26 → 12 26\to 12 , AF3 0 → 0 0\to 0 , MF 6 → 0 6\to 0 ) while lifting the Geminis to 92 92 and 99 % 99\% . These three probes point to an absence failure: the model does not appear to form the required conclusion. Structure shows the opposite pattern. Although the final answer is wrong, the correct conclusion becomes decodable on 93% of items at an intermediate layer before weakening toward the output. This is a loss failure, the represented-but-unused pattern reported for speech prosody [ 11 ] : useful information is formed internally but does not reliably reach the final prediction. Notably, structure is also the task on which Qwen remains robust to greater derivation depth, reaching 90% at d2, linking stronger internal representation with greater behavioral robustness. If a conclusion is formed but lost, externalizing it may help; we test this next. Figure 3: Logit lens on Qwen2.5-Omni: log-probability margin between the correct and incorrect answer words decoded from each layer. With derivation required the margin never leaves zero for modulation (d2, n = 72 n{=}72 items) but rises to + 0.9 +0.9 at layer 25 25 for structure (F4, n = 30 n{=}30 ) before falling at the output. Finding 6. Explicit intermediate reasoning helps selectively, but does not solve the problem. d1 d2 d3 Mod. 76 → 79 76{\to}79 26 → 0 26{\to}0 0 → 0 0{\to}0 Cad. 83 → 83 83{\to}83 17 → 42 17{\to}42 17 → 8 17{\to}8 Struct. 100 → 62 100{\to}62 90 → 38 90{\to}38 40 → 43 40{\to}43 Table 5: Two-call mitigation, Qwen2.5-Omni: pair accuracy (%), single → \to two-call, n = 72 n{=}72 . Column color: reasoning depth; cell color: direction of change. The two-call procedure (Sec. 2 ) helps only selectively (Table 5 ). Cadence d2 improves from 17 % 17\% to 42 % 42\% , and the failing structure full report on the battery from 0 % 0\% to 17 % 17\% . But deeper derivations are not rescued: modulation d3 remains at 0 % 0\% , while cadence d3 falls from 17 % 17\% to 8 % 8\% . The procedure can also destroy information that was previously usable: structure d1 drops from 100 % 100\% to 62 % 62\% and d2 from 90 % 90\% to 38 % 38\% when the intermediate summary omits the score the second call needs. Externalizing the intermediate step helps in a few cells, hurts in others, and does not extend the model’s reasoning depth.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: Given an MIR tool’s output, current audio-language models copy a stated conclusion but rarely derive one, and the loss grows with every reasoning step left to them. Our results motivate evaluating tool-augmented audio systems not only by whether they retrieve the right information, but also by how much derivation they leave to the language model and whether that derivation is performed reliably. This also suggests a training direction: post-training should reward not only correct tool calling , but also correct tool reading , that is, interpreting and reasoning over the returned output before answering. Derivation-depth examples and flipped-conclusion controls could provide supervision or reward signals for this capability, while also testing whether models verify rather than simply follow tool outputs. Future work will extend these ideas to broader model families and musical systems, including non-Western traditions.

sections.heading: 6 Compliance with ethical standards
sections.text: All non-synthetic audio is from GuitarSet [ 14 ] (CC BY 4.0); the remaining stimuli are synthetic renders of programmatically generated scores and carry no third-party rights. The human listening baseline was collected from one consenting adult musician with no personal data recorded. No IRB review was required. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) assisted with generating the figures and with editing the manuscript for grammar and phrasing; the authors reviewed all content and take full responsibility for its correctness.

Improving the MIR tool alone is insufficient when the downstream model cannot reliably transform its measurements into the requested conclusion. In summary, our contributions are a controlled framework for measuring derivation depth , evidence that even elementary derivations fail despite available musical knowledge , and mechanistic evidence distinguishing conclusions that are never formed from those that are formed but lost before output . 2 Method and Experiments Experiments fix the musical fact and varies only how it reaches the model: report format, audio, and reasoning distance. 2.1 Setup Tasks. Each task is a minimal pair: two versions of a piece differing in exactly one musical property, which isolates that property as the sole determinant of the correct answer. The five tasks are cadence (authentic vs. deceptive), modulation (new major vs. minor key), scale (Lydian vs. Ionian, one note apart), motif (transposed return vs. a new motif) and structure (ABA vs. through-composed). Each targets a property a standard MIR tool reports. All battery items are synthetic: short scores written to exhibit exactly one property are generated programmatically as MIDI and rendered to audio with FluidSynth (TimGM6mb General MIDI soundfont, piano), and the template report is filled from the known score, so ground truth is exact. Each task has N = 6 N{=}6 compositions rendered at up to five transpositions between − 6 -6 and + 6 +6 semitones, giving up to 30 30 pairs per task ( 23 23 for scale). For each item we express the same musical information in six forms that reflect how an MIR measurement may appear in a tool-augmented system (Table 1 ). F1 and F3 state the conclusion; F2 gives the single value it follows from; F4 to F6 give the full tool output with increasing clutter (F5) and structure (F6). F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} states the wrong conclusion in F1’s form, to test whether a model follows the report even against the correct answer. Derivation ladder. To order the formats by reasoning distance, we generate 72 72 items per task in which the same fact is reported at four depths: d0 states the conclusion; d1 gives the fact one step away (for modulation, the home and new key); d2 gives the evidence for that fact (the pivot chord); d3 gives only its constituents (the chord’s pitches). Items vary key and harmonic relation rather than transposition, so every report is distinct, and intervals for the ladder resample items. Real tool output and real recordings. We rebuild all six formats for modulation and structure from a running librosa [ 8 ] analyzer on the same audio, so the report is a real tool’s output rather than a template. Separately, on 60 60 GuitarSet [ 14 ] recordings with expert key annotations, we ask for the key from audio alone, with the annotation supplied as the tool output, and with a deliberately wrong annotation. Models and input conditions. We test three open-weight models run locally, Qwen2.5-Omni [ 15 ] , Music Flamingo (MF) [ 4 ] , and Audio Flamingo 3 (AF3) [ 5 ] , and two API models, Gemini 2.5 Flash [ 2 ] and Gemini 3.6 Flash [ 6 ] . We run every format in two conditions: no-audio, where the model sees only the measurement, which isolates whether it can read the measurement on its own; and audio-crossed, where the model also gets the audio, which tests whether audio helps when reasoning from the measurement fails. Scoring. Each test item is a matched pair containing both alternatives of the task (e.g., one major-key modulation and one minor-key modulation). A pair is counted as correct only when the model answers both members correctly. Because the two members have opposite correct answers, a model that always gives the same response is correct on at most one of them and scores 0 % 0\% pair accuracy; chance is 25 % 25\% . We report 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples over base compositions. We resample compositions rather than individual transpositions because transpositions of the same composition are not independent. We validated automatic keyword scoring against 100 manually scored responses, achieving κ = 0.90 \kappa=0.90 agreement. Knowledge probes. To separate a missing fact from a failure to combine facts already present, we ask each fact the modulation ladder needs alone, with terse answer-only questions ( 48 48 items each): whether a named key is major or minor (needed at d1); which key a dominant seventh resolves to and whether a scale degree is major or minor (d2); which chord a set of pitches spells (d3). To check that a terse probe does not understate knowledge, the d2 rule is also asked with the rule stated, as multiple choice, and with reasoning permitted. Mechanistic probes. Behavioral failure alone cannot tell us whether Qwen2.5-Omni never computes an answer or computes one it fails to use. We test this on two conditions already in the behavioral evaluation: conclusion stated (modulation d0, structure F1) and derivation required (modulation d2, 72 72 items; structure F4, 30 30 items). Since the derivation-required condition often declines to answer, we append a fixed continuation (“The new key is”, “The third section”) and read the residual stream at the answer position. A logit lens [ 9 ] projects that stream through the output head at every layer, tracking the model’s preference between the two candidate answers: a conclusion that is present should be decodable before the final layer. Activation steering [ 13 ] tests whether the state that encodes the correct conclusion can rescue a failing derivation: for modulation, we inject the mean hidden-state difference between the two conditions, computed leave-one-out over items, into the derivation-required forward pass at one of seven layers and several strengths, and measure accuracy. As a control, we also state the required musical rule in the prompt (Fig. 3 ). Two-call mitigation. If a derivation is never performed, forcing it into the transcript should help. We test this with a two-call procedure: in the first call, the model states what the measurement says and what it indicates; in the second call, it answers using only its own first-call statement, with the original measurement withheld. This differs from ordinary chain-of-thought prompting [ 1 ] , where the model can still fall back on the original evidence. 3 Results and Discussion Finding 1. Models follow stated conclusions, even when they are wrong. When the tool output states the conclusion (F1/F3), all models are near-perfect. But when we deliberately flip that conclusion in F1 ¯ \overline{\mathrm{F1}} , accuracy falls to 0 % 0\% for every model, the frontier models included (Table 2 , last column): each follows the incorrect statement, even when audio is available. Thus, the models read the tool output but do not reliably verify its conclusion. Accuracy falls with the distance between tool output and answer; one reasoning step is enough. The format profile. The gap appears as soon as the tool provides measurements rather than the answer itself (Table 2 ). In the no-audio condition, open-model accuracy drops from 100 % → ∼ 35 % 100\%\to{\sim}35\% , while the Gemini models show a smaller but consistent drop. Providing the relevant tool output is therefore not sufficient; performance depends on how much reasoning remains between that output and the answer. Modulation F2 reveals one confound: it gives the new key but not the home key, so the output alone does not establish that a modulation occurred. We therefore use a controlled derivation ladder in which every rung contains sufficient information, while only the number of reasoning steps changes. The derivation ladder. We fix the musical fact and vary how many reasoning steps separate the tool output from the answer (Fig. 2 , Table 3 ). On modulation, all three open models score 100 % 100\% when the report states the conclusion (d0). Replacing the conclusion with the new key, “D major,” leaves one step: recognizing that D major is a major key. Accuracy falls to as low as 57 % 57\% . Giving the secondary dominant instead (d2) drops it to 0 0 – 26 % 26\% , at or below chance. Giving only its pitches (d3) drops it to 0 % 0\% . At every depth the question is the same, whether the new key is major or minor, and so is the answer: major (D major). Cadence and structure follow the same trend, though the step where models fail differs by task. The limitation appears before any long chain of reasoning. One elementary step between tool output and answer already costs up to 43 43 points. The frontier models split on the hardest chain: Gemini 2.5 Flash collapses at d2 like the open models ( 15 % 15\% ), while Gemini 3.6 Flash, which reasons internally before answering, holds 86 86 and 82 % 82\% at d2 and d3; both are at or near 100 % 100\% on every cadence and structure rung. The first-step failure is not a knowledge gap A natural explanation for the depth drop is missing music-theory knowledge. We test the required intermediate facts directly (Table 3 , right block). At d1, all three open models identify whether a named key is major or minor with 100% accuracy, yet score as low as 57% when that same fact must be used to answer the modulation question. Thus, even the first-step failure reflects difficulty applying available knowledge to the tool output, not simply missing knowledge. At deeper levels, both effects appear: some models lack the required theory, while others know the intermediate facts but still fail to combine them. Derivation fails either because the conclusion is never formed or because it is lost. The mechanistic probes reveal two distinct failure modes (Fig. 3 ). For modulation, the correct answer never becomes reliably decodable at any layer when derivation is required. Activation steering does not recover it (Qwen moves from 25 % 25\% to at most 29 % 29\% across seven layers), and stating the required rule in the prompt moves the open models nowhere (Qwen 26 → 12 26\to 12 , AF3 0 → 0 0\to 0 , MF 6 → 0 6\to 0 ) while lifting the Geminis to 92 92 and 99 % 99\% . These three probes point to an absence failure: the model does not appear to form the required conclusion. Structure shows the opposite pattern. Although the final answer is wrong, the correct conclusion becomes decodable on 93% of items at an intermediate layer before weakening toward the output. This is a loss failure, the represented-but-unused pattern reported for speech prosody [ 11 ] : useful information is formed internally but does not reliably reach the final prediction. Notably, structure is also the task on which Qwen remains robust to greater derivation depth, reaching 90% at d2, linking stronger internal representation with greater behavioral robustness. If a conclusion is formed but lost, externalizing it may help; we test this next. Cadence d2 improves from 17 % 17\% to 42 % 42\% , and the failing structure full report on the battery from 0 % 0\% to 17 % 17\% . The procedure can also destroy information that was previously usable: structure d1 drops from 100 % 100\% to 62 % 62\% and d2 from 90 % 90\% to 38 % 38\% when the intermediate summary omits the score the second call needs. Externalizing the intermediate step helps in a few cells, hurts in others, and does not extend the model’s reasoning depth. 4 Conclusion Given an MIR tool’s output, current audio-language models copy a stated conclusion but rarely derive one, and the loss grows with every reasoning step left to them. Our results motivate evaluating tool-augmented audio systems not only by whether they retrieve the right information, but also by how much derivation they leave to the language model and whether that derivation is performed reliably. This also suggests a training direction: post-training should reward not only correct tool calling , but also correct tool reading , that is, interpreting and reasoning over the returned output before answering. Derivation-depth examples and flipped-conclusion controls could provide supervision or reward signals for this capability, while also testing whether models verify rather than simply follow tool outputs.
